messages.content: Write a post about why a company is investing in developer relations. Around 250 words.

**Why we're hiring a developer relations team**

Last quarter we read every support ticket filed in someone's first week with us. Two hundred and nine of them. About a third came from people trying to do something our docs never mentioned. Another third came from people who found the right page and misread it, which is on us.

That's the argument.

We sell to developers, and developers don't get sold to. They try something on a Tuesday night, hit a wall, and either work around it or quietly go elsewhere. Nobody files a ticket that says "I gave up." We only ever hear from the ones who stayed.

The people who change that outcome aren't in sales. They're the ones who write the sample app that actually compiles, who sit in the Discord at 11pm, who come back to engineering and say four different people tripped on the same auth flow this week.

We've been doing this in the margins — an engineer writing a post between sprints, a PM answering GitHub issues on a Saturday. It doesn't scale, and it wears people down.

So: three roles, reporting into product rather than marketing. The reporting line is the whole design. Under marketing, developer relations turns into a content calendar and a conference booth. Under product, what DevRel learns has somewhere to go.

We'll know it worked by two numbers: median time to a developer's first successful API call, and the share of documentation bugs we catch before a customer does. Impressions are not on the list.

---

That's the case, right there.

Our customers are developers, and developers don't want to be sold to. They try something on a Tuesday night, hit a wall, and either route around it or drift away without saying anything. No one files a ticket titled "I gave up." We only hear from the people who stuck it out.

The people who move that number aren't in sales. They're the ones who write the sample app that actually builds, who are in the Discord at 11pm, who walk back to engineering and mention that four separate people snagged on the same auth flow this week.

We've been covering this off the side of a desk — an engineer writing a post between sprints, a PM working through GitHub issues on a Saturday. It doesn't scale, and it grinds people down.

So: three roles, reporting into product instead of marketing. That reporting line is the point. Under marketing, developer relations collapses into a content calendar and a booth at a conference. Under product, what the team learns lands somewhere that can act on it.

Two numbers will tell us whether it worked: median time to a developer's first successful API call, and the share of doc bugs we find before a customer does. Impressions aren't on the list.
